analysis.one_liner: Pays firefighters up to $1 million for PFAS-linked cancer, funded by taxes on PFAS makers.
analysis.headline: Sen. Booker's bill to compensate firefighters with PFAS-related cancer, paid for by a 10% tax on PFAS products and PFAS litigation settlements, got no cosponsors, no committee hearing, and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a no-fault compensation program for firefighters who get sick from PFAS, the "forever chemicals" found in firefighting foam and protective gear. A firefighter with 2 or more years of service who develops a listed PFAS-related condition — kidney, testicular, prostate, bladder, pancreatic, and other cancers, thyroid disease, or ulcerative colitis — could claim a cash award without going to court or proving anyone was negligent. The money would come from a dedicated trust fund financed by a new 10% excise tax on PFAS products and a 10% tax on companies paying PFAS litigation settlements. The bill was introduced in March 2024, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Firefighters — civilian, military, and volunteer — with at least two years of service who develop PFAS-related cancers or other listed illnesses, and the families of firefighters who died of them. The bill assumes firefighting exposure caused the condition, so a claimant would not need to prove how or where the exposure happened. Awards start at $250,000 for a cancer diagnosis and $50,000 for a non-cancer condition, multiplied by years of service up to 4x — meaning a firefighter with 10 or more years on the job and a PFAS-linked cancer could receive up to $1 million.

how_it_helps.text: The program is no-fault: the government must presume any listed PFAS-related condition in a firefighter was caused by firefighting exposure and may not consider negligence or liability defenses, sparing sick firefighters the burden of a lawsuit.

Base awards are $250,000 for a PFAS-related cancer and $50,000 for a non-cancer condition, multiplied by a service modifier of 1 to 4 based on years of service — so a 10-year veteran with cancer could receive up to $1 million.
The program covers civilian, military, and volunteer firefighters, and the families of deceased firefighters can file claims; compensation is protected from a deceased firefighter's creditors.

The fund would be financed by a dedicated 10% excise tax on PFAS products (including firefighting gear) and a 10% excise tax on payments made under PFAS litigation settlements and final court orders, rather than general taxpayer revenue.
Claimants dissatisfied with an award can appeal for fresh review in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims, and attorneys who overcharge claimants face statutory penalties.

analysis.who_pays: PFAS manufacturers and importers, who would pay 10% of the sales price of every PFAS product; and any company paying a PFAS-related litigation settlement or court judgment, which would owe 10% of its value. Those costs would partly pass through to customers, including fire departments buying PFAS-containing gear.

drawbacks.text: If trust fund money runs short, the bill requires payments to be prorated — meaning sick firefighters could receive reduced awards until more money comes in, with 6% annual interest added on the delayed balance.

The no-fault rule presumes that any listed condition was caused by firefighting exposure, even though PFAS exposure is widespread in the general environment, so some awards could go to people whose illness had other causes.
The 10% tax on PFAS products, including firefighting gear, would raise prices for the fire departments and manufacturers that buy or sell that equipment.

Claims are tightly limited: only one claim per firefighter, one cancer and one non-cancer condition each, a two-year filing window tied to final regulations, and only firefighters with two or more years of service qualify.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the firefighters and families the program serves, the benefit is substantial: cash awards without the cost, delay, and risk of proving causation in court. The main design weakness is funding — the trust fund depends entirely on the new excise taxes, and the bill itself anticipates that claims could exceed the money available and requires reduced payments in that case. The excise taxes would also raise costs for PFAS-using industries, which is the point of the bill but a real cost that could partly land on buyers of PFAS-containing products.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate in March 2024, referred to the Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the Firefighter PFAS Injury Compensation Act of 2024 in the Senate on March 21, 2024.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the day it was introduced; that referral was the only action the bill ever received.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor, and the Finance Committee took no further action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and companies paying PFAS litigation settlements are better off, because the 10% excise taxes that would have funded compensation never took effect. Firefighters with PFAS-related illnesses gained nothing; they are left to rely on lawsuits or state remedies instead of the federal no-fault program.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey and the bill's sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee, where it received no further action

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it sat without action until the Congress ended

against.name: PFAS manufacturers and other litigation defendants
against.role: Chemical companies and other defendants facing PFAS liability
against.what_they_did: Companies facing large PFAS liabilities have broadly opposed measures that expand PFAS accountability and add costs to PFAS sales and settlements; the congressional record contains no documented activity by them on this specific bill

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no party breakdown exists; the bill had a Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would impose a 10% excise tax on the sales price of every PFAS product, directly reducing the revenue of companies that make or import PFAS chemicals and goods. The same companies face billions in PFAS injury and contamination lawsuits, so the tax and the litigation-settlement tax cut directly against their financial interest while the fund's compensation protects exposed firefighters.

A second 10% excise tax would apply to the present value of any qualifying PFAS litigation award — payments under final court orders or settlements to compensate for PFAS exposure harm, other than personal injury claims. This adds a direct cost to settling PFAS lawsuits.

Firefighter gear containing PFAS is explicitly listed as a taxed PFAS product, so turnout-gear makers would owe the 10% sales tax and could pass the cost to fire departments. Firefighters themselves are the bill's beneficiaries even as their gear is a taxed product.
